speaker: The Chairman
text: Head J, Ministry of Defence, Mr Vikram Nair.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The last year has seen global tensions rise on multiple fronts.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The rivalry between China and the United States (US) is playing out on many fronts, including the South China Sea, in the context of a trade war and even over the Fifth Generation (5G) network and the next generation of technologies.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The tensions between Russia and the West are also continuing, with President Putin recently declaring he is ready for another Cuban missile crisis if the US wants one.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: These great power rivalries have always had repercussions for the rest of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While Singapore tries to maintain friendships with as many people as possible, this may not always be easy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Just up north, in Malaysia, the last two weeks have seen a tussle for the premiership, which has resulted in a change of Prime Minister and change of government.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: While Prime Minister Muhyiddin was sworn in yesterday, there seems to be further unrest on the streets and the new Prime Minister may well face a challenge, such as a vote of no-confidence in the next Parliament sitting.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Typically, when there is unrest in our neighbouring countries, governments may feel under pressure to become more nationalistic and this may adversely affect relationships with other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: At the same time, unconventional threats are growing.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Threats to cybersecurity and fake news threaten to subvert our systems from the inside.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: A classic example was during the early days of the Coronavirus Disease of 2019 (COVID-19) when panic was being triggered by messages that misstated the implications of Disease Outbreak Response System Condition (DORSCON) Orange and suggested people stockpile to avoid shortages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: Ironically, it was messages like these that triggered the panic which resulted in the temporary shortages.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In the Middle East, tensions between the US and Iran are escalating and the disputes between Saudi Arabia and Iran as well as Saudi Arabia and Qatar continues.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Islamic State of Iraq and Syria (ISIS) remains a threat and continues to hold territory and both carry out and inspire attacks in other countries.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The Singapore Armed Forces (SAF) has been the backbone of our national defence.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: It clearly faces a wide range of threats and contingencies it needs to prepare for.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: The only way forward for SAF is to evolve, to invest in technology so that we can do more with less resources.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: There have been some exciting announcements of big ticket acquisitions in recent times.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: In relation to manpower, plans have been announced to develop a hybrid force, so that more and more unmanned technologies will be able to replace men in the fighting force.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair (Sembawang)
text: I would be grateful if the Minister for Defence could provide us more generally with details on the Ministry of Defence's (MINDEF's) plans to ensure the Next-Generation SAF continues to be effective and capable of safeguarding Singapore's national security.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Henry Kwek, take both your cuts together.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Chairman, Sir, last year, I had the opportunity to visit the SAF's training camp in Brunei.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: It was heartening to see the dedication of our servicemen who had to man our overseas detachment and to facilitate the training of our visiting SAF soldiers.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Over the years, going on overseas training has become a part of what it means to be a member of the SAF, whether it is a regular, full-time National Serviceman (NSF) or National Serviceman (NSMan).

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: We train overseas because we need to overcome our space constraints to give our people better and more realistic training opportunities in diverse environments.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MINDEF and SAF have worked hard with our partners to provide SAF access to overseas training facilities.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Could the Minister for Defence please provide more information on RSAF's Guam Detachment and how it will improve on RSAF's training?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At last year's Committee of Supply (COS) debate, MINDEF announced the intention to purchase the F-35, a fifth generation (5G) multi-role aircraft, which can provide air-to-air, air-to-ground and intelligence, surveillance and reconnaissance (ISR) missions.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: The F-35's stealth capabilities can help us maintain air dominance and overcome sophisticated air defences.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: At the same time, the F-35s can fuse sensors and information from different sources, thereby networking our 4G aircrafts and SAF assets altogether.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: MINDEF recently announced that Singapore has received the US' approval for the sale of F-35s to Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry (Nee Soon)
text: Could MINDEF please provide an update on Singapore's acquisition of the F-35s, including how the F-35s will improve the capabilities of SAF?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, for more than 200 years, sea trade has been vital to Singapore's economy.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Singapore is one of the busiest transshipment hubs in the world and it is important for us to maintain our sea lines of communication.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, the Malaysian government did not escalate matters and the Malaysian Navy never got involved in this dispute.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: This is likely because the Singapore Navy is strong and it was clear it would have been able to defend Singapore if necessary.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Threats like these may reduce the confidence of people using our sea lanes.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: What are MINDEF and SAF doing to secure our waters?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Mr Chairman, East Asia is again becoming a site for more intense power contestation, particularly in the South China Sea.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Worryingly, some of this competition is taking on more militarised characteristics region-wide.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Such developments have the unfortunate consequence of prompting other regional actors to adopt more militarised stances.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: They include arms acquisitions and more muscular positions over disputes.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: These developments challenge stability and freedom of access, even if they do not directly involve Singapore.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Could the Minister for Defence update the House on the Government's strategy for navigating this increasingly complicated security landscape?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: Deterrence alone cannot fully address these concerns, and defence spending needs to be within prudent limits.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim (Aljunied)
text: In particular, what role should be played by SAF on a routine basis and during contingencies and how is SAF working towards these objectives?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore's approach to defence is shaped by both the unique circumstances surrounding our country's Independence and the enduring geostrategic limitations we face.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Given our strategic circumstances, a strong defence is necessary to ensure that we enjoy peace and stability and that our sovereignty and territorial integrity are protected.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: In order to defend our sovereignty and promote our national interests, Singapore has worked closely with our international partners to build a stable regional architecture.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Despite the challenges involved in navigating an increasingly complex security environment, Singapore has continued to forge strong relations with our key partners, such as the US and China.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How is MINDEF working with our key defence partners to enhance cooperation and address common security challenges?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: Singapore is a good friend of both the US and China.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The US is our major security and economic partner.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: The size and scale of US investments in Singapore far outstrip any other country's.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: With China, Singapore has established an "All-Round Cooperative Partnership Progressing with the Times".

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: But we must be clear-eyed about our own national interests and understand the Government's considerations when we adopt principled positions on bilateral, regional or international issues.

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we continue to engage the US and China in our security collaborations?

speaker: Mr Desmond Choo (Tampines)
text: How do we continue to build upon this?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Mr Chairman, at last year's COS debate, the Minister spoke about MINDEF's successful chairmanship of the ADMM and the ADMM plus eight dialogue partner countries (ADMM-Plus) in 2018.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: MINDEF has worked hard to ensure that should the need arise, our Armed Forces will be able to defend Singapore against both conventional and unconventional threats.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: However, the better way to deal with these threats is to do what we can to ensure that they do not arise in the first place.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: To that end, as ironic as it may appear, SAF will be truly successful if we never actually need to call on our servicemen and servicewomen to defend Singapore in a time of conflict.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Could the Minister provide an update on what MINDEF is doing to ensure that the region remains stable and peaceful?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Australia is a close and valued defence partner and the signing of the CSP was a clear demonstration of the relationship we enjoy with our Australian friends.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: While we have had an excellent defence relationship with Australia for many years, CSP provides a framework for the further deepening of defence engagements between our two countries.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: We have already been having our troops trained in Australia for many years.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Many of our troops have trained in the Shoalwater Bay training area.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: I know that we are very appreciative of the support provided by the Australian government and the Australian defence force.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: However, with the recent bush fires in the east coast of Australia, could the Minister let us know if the Shoalwater Bay training area has been affected and whether this has had an impact on the SAF's ability to fully utilise the area as a training ground?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: In particular, I imagine that the dry conditions and the threat of fires could have had an impact on our use of ordnance and ammunition which would have been a significant reason for using the Shoalwater Bay training area in the first place, and for us committing to spend on developing military facilities there.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: Coming back to the CSP, this also provides for even greater access to training areas in Australia for our troops.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong (Punggol East)
text: And I would like to ask the Minister if he can provide an update on the enhancements to training facilities, including both in the Shoalwater Bay training area as the new Townsville field training area and how the CSP can improve the SAF's training effectiveness.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Unconventional security threats, such as terrorism, pose increasingly greater risks to our nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: The ongoing turmoil in the Middle East provides opportunities for terrorist groups to step up attacks, not just there, but also close to home.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Singapore is not insulated from the influences of returning foreign fighters.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Given the threats from terrorism abroad, would the Ministry share with the House an update on its efforts to counter terrorism?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: What measures have been implemented to limit their ability to propagate their radical messages and minimise their influence on our communities?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In addition, how does the Ministry identify, prevent and monitor potential fighters entering Singapore?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: For Singaporeans and foreign residents and workers here who may be radicalised, do we have adequate surveillance measures and resources to spot, monitor and contain them?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: How does MINDEF restrict access to such materials in order to minimise potential injuries, deaths and damage?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: In recent attacks overseas, we have also observed the use of common tools, such as knives and even vehicles, by terrorists to launch attacks on innocent bystanders.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira (Tanjong Pagar)
text: Do we have in place an early alert-and-response system to detect behavioural anomalies which will trigger alerts and calls for urgent assistance?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, at last year's National Day Rally, Prime Minister Lee spoke about how climate change is one of the gravest challenges we are facing.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: I quote, "Both the SAF and climate change defences are existential for Singapore.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: These are life and death matters." The greatest threat is from rising sea levels, which will erode the shorelines of our small island unless mitigating action is taken.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Areas at risk and which require priority protection include our military installations, the airport, the Central Business District, and the industrial estates of Jurong and Tuas.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Global warming has also resulted in the weather becoming more extreme.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Singapore has become hotter with prolonged dry spells even as we experience bursts of heavier rainfall.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: One concern is about mitigating the impact of these dry periods on our reservoirs.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We also need to consider collaborative measures with Malaysia to protect the reservoirs there which supply us with water.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: We have to plan for ways to protect people and minimise the potential damage to our facilities from flooding and toppling trees during heavy downpours and storms.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: In short, a well-coordinated national effort is needed to respond to economic, social and military defence challenges related to climate change.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Would the Minister elaborate on what are some of the measures taken by MINDEF and SAF to address these concerns?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Chairman, Singapore is a low-lying island nation that is vulnerable to rising sea levels as a result of climate change.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: Mitigating actions being considered include major engineering works, such as empoldering and reclamation of offshore islands and coastal adaptation initiatives, such as planting mangroves.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: While Singapore has had experience with the traditional land reclamation method, empoldering is new to us.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: It involves building a dyke around the area to be reclaimed and draining water from within it.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: The reclaimed low-lying land, known as a polder, will be below sea level, kept dry by the sea wall.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: What lessons are we gaining from this building experience for the future use of this technique in other reclamation areas?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong (Bishan-Toa Payoh)
text: How does this technique compare with the traditional land reclamation method in terms of construction and maintenance costs, as well as benefits and risks?

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Chairman, SAF performs an important role in deterring potential aggressors and protecting Singapore.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As a small country, we are at a natural disadvantage when it comes to our defence while, at the same time, defence is existential.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: We have traditionally compensated for our small size by spending more on defence and investing in the best and latest technologies, while at the same time, building good defence relations with a wide range of countries, including all our neighbours as well as some of the middle and great powers, including the US.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: However, in recent years, defence spending has been rising all around the region and in many other parts of the world.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: As larger countries also invest and strengthen their forces, our technological edge may diminish and I expect there will be pressure on us to spend more to keep up with them.

speaker: Mr Vikram Nair
text: Do they envision a long-term increase in our defence budget to keep up with these rising demands?

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Mr Chairman, we are a small city-state with an open economy and are, therefore, vulnerable to external factors.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: As the Minister for Defence Dr Ng Eng Hen has reiterated over the past years, Singapore cannot fail in its frontline defence to protect our sovereignty.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Through the past efforts of our predecessors, our SAF is now one of the more modernised armed forces in the region with superior equipment and stronger fighting power.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: MINDEF previously announced its plans to building a modernised tri-service SAF which include acquiring F-35S Joint Strike Fighter jets to replace the current F-16 fighter jets, acquiring new Invincible-class submarines and multi-role combat vessels as well as new next-generation Armoured Fighting Vehicles for our defence forces.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: The importance of maintaining a strong SAF and the need to be accountable to taxpayers requires a balance.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: In light of the current economic slowdown where we are seeing enterprises struggle to stay in business, the debate on whether we should be spending so much of our taxpayers' money on Singapore's defence or if the money is more well spent aiding our local enterprises will no doubt resurface in the minds of many.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister share how sustainable it is to spend to modernise and can the Minister explain what is MINDEF doing to ensure that every dollar of the defence budget is spent wisely and prudently?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Chairman, MINDEF previously informed Parliament how it attempts to maximise Singapore's defence dollars, through the purchase of only items it needs, retrofitting existing assets and so on.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Could the Minister for Defence elaborate also on its acquisition decisions – how MINDEF assesses the reasonableness of the prices quoted by vendors and ensures that it receives fair value for money on its purchases?

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: At stake in these decisions are hundreds of millions or even billions of dollars.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: More importantly, they involve the lives and safety of our men and women in uniform and, ultimately, Singapore's security.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: A key issue is that unlike other products and services involved in Government procurement, defence articles may not be freely market-tested due to the confidentiality of specifications or dependence on specialist contractors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Systems sold at a certain price point may be subject to expensive after-sales maintenance and upgrade packages with proprietary and protected information.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: After all, contemporary defence platforms can be highly tailored and involve the integration of multiple systems overseen by large numbers of vendors and subcontractors.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: This is just one well-known example about a single programme.

speaker: Ms Sylvia Lim
text: Can MINDEF elaborate on how it injects rigour into its procurement decisions to ensure value for money?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Mr Chairman, all of us have either served in SAF or have a child, parent, relative or close friend who has been in the SAF.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: SAF is an intrinsic part of Singapore and is part of our identity as Singaporeans.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Part of why SAF has been successful has been the trust which exists between Singaporeans and SAF.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: SAF enjoys broad support among citizens and we all understand why we need to have mandatory National Service (NS), even if it comes at a cost to personal pursuits in academia, sports and other areas.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: However, when parents send their sons off to enlist in the SAF or when children bid goodbye to a parent who is going for in-camp training, there is an expectation, a very legitimate expectation, if I may say, that the SAF has done everything possible to ensure that they return home safely.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Unfortunately, as is well-known to Members, there have been several training incidents over the last few years, some of which have led to deaths of our servicemen.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Could the Minister provide an update on the work of the IGO, including how many instances of unsafe practices the IGO has identified in the past year and what real steps have been taken to address these?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Has training safety in the SAF improved since the IGO was set up, and have additional safety measures been introduced?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: These findings demonstrate that training safety cannot just be a matter of safety guidelines and regulations, but must be part of the SAF's organisational culture and practised by every soldier at every level.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy (Nominated Member)
text: Can the Minister share how is the SAF instilling safety consciousness and personal responsibility for one's safety amongst NSmen on the ground?

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Mr Chairman, even as we aim for zero training fatalities, it is inherent in the nature of the SAF that accidents will probably happen and the challenge for us then is to ensure that when they do happen, that our service personnel have the very best medical care which we can provide for them.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: The SAF Medical Corp has been around for over 50 years now and has developed into a professionally run and managed medical service for our servicemen and women.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: It is, however, important that the medical capabilities of the SAF are continually updated and upgraded to ensure that medical support for our troops is up to date, both in terms of practice and procedure as well as in equipment and technology.

speaker: Mr Charles Chong
text: Could the Minister provide some insights as to how SAF is improving its capabilities to respond to medical emergencies and what steps are being taken by SAF to ensure that the SAF Medical Corp continues to provide the medical support which our servicemen and servicewomen require?

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong, take your three cuts together.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, the profile of Singapore’s population has evolved over time.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Our demography is made up of people from increasingly varied backgrounds.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Today, we have a larger proportion of children born to interracial and transnational marriages.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: We also have many Singaporeans who have been born and lived overseas for a number of years, Permanent Residents (PRs) and new citizens from many different nationalities.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: This means that our NS resource has become increasingly diverse.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: NS is particularly a challenge for our young men who have spent extended periods of time overseas.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Are there specific orientation programmes to help them adjust to the cultural differences?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: How are MINDEF and SAF helping our NSmen from such diverse backgrounds understand the need for NS and adjust to NS?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Most importantly, how does SAF build a sense of unity and solidarity among these cohorts?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, our servicemen make much sacrifice towards NS.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In order to train and remain fit and ready for their duties, they have to make sacrifices in the areas of their personal and work life.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is important that MINDEF and SAF do their best to help ease the burdens on our servicemen as much as possible.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Would the Ministry consider tapping on technology and closer collaboration with employers and even other Government agencies to enable systematic collation of feedback and harness suggestions on areas of key concern, such as childcare and eldercare?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: The purpose of this suggestion is to enable 360-degree support for our servicemen so that they can better focus on their military duties when in camps, knowing that the other areas of their lives are well supported and taken care of.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: While much emphasis is placed on the two years as an NSF, it is also important to keep in mind that the entire NS experience also includes the time that the men of Singapore spend as pre-enlistees and Operationally-Ready NSmen.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Their experience will also influence and have an impact on the next generation of our young who are watching and getting ready to serve the nation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: How are MINDEF and SAF working to enhance the NS experience for our NSmen at different stages of their NS journey?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: How can the Ministry tap upon their interests, aptitudes and experiences over the years to serve our nation better?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Chairman, all young male Singaporeans have to commit two years in the prime of their lives for service to our nation.

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: It is important that we recognise their commitments and contributions, and do our utmost to support them as they prepare for further studies or entry to the workforce as they near their Operationally Ready Date (ORD).

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Is there any way that MINDEF can assist to coordinate areas of synergy so that the courses are both relevant to the NSF's role in SAF and their areas of interest?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: In addition, will the effectiveness of these programmes be monitored and reviewed?

speaker: Mr Chong Kee Hiong
text: Does the Ministry also take into account feedback and suggestions from the NSFs, education institutions and employers about the usefulness of these initiatives and how improvements can be incorporated over time?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, many Singaporeans go online for all their needs.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Our digital connectivity provides opportunities for MINDEF to reach out and engage both the military and civilian forces in joint initiatives.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: What plans does the Ministry have to further exploit technology to enhance cooperation between both stakeholders for our security?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Would the Minister also share how we are leveraging technology to enhance our soldiers' NS experience and well-being?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Technological advances have changed defence strategies and training methods around the world.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Would the Ministry share how these technological developments have impacted SAF?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Are we adequately prepared to handle increasingly sophisticated and complex equipment?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: What are the main challenges in securing access to such technologies?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How are we progressing in our proprietary defence research and development?

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy
text: Every male Singaporean has to commit two years of his youth to serve the country.

speaker: Mr Arasu Duraisamy
text: We must provide a seamless and convenient means for young male Singaporeans to prepare for enlistment.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Amidst rising threats of terrorism, cyberattacks and other challenges, we will need to evolve our approach towards NS.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: To this end, the NS experience must be constantly shaped and reshaped to address the pressures, demands and desires of our future economy and future generations.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Everyone, meaning all Singaporeans, our institutions and community, has a role to play in ensuring we have a robust NS system.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Thus, our families, employers, schools and community groups are key pillars of support so that our servicemen can focus on their training.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Many of us have seen and participated in the regular SAF community engagement projects.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: The Army, Navy and Air Force have open house carnivals to engage the public as well as school partnership programmes to engage the students.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: Besides that, National Education and Total Defence Day is also part of the school’s curriculum.

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: How about new employers, including those who are newly posted to run operations located here in Singapore?

speaker: Mr Ang Hin Kee (Ang Mo Kio)
text: This will ensure that our reservists will similarly be well-supported and their role well-understood.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Mr Chairman, NS is now seen as a rite of passage in every Singaporean man’s life, but the journey does not stop after the NSF’s ORD.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: As a Singaporean son, I myself have been through the whole cycle and can testify that it is, indeed, a unique experience for all.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: My son Donavan has just joined me on this journey of ORNS.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: I have three more boys who will be joining on this journey soon.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: However, serving two years of NS means pushing back one’s plan for education or career.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: The people living in Singapore, regardless of whether they are citizens or foreigners working here are indirectly benefiting from the sacrifices of our Singaporean Sons, we hope that all will recognise and appreciate the sacrifices made by them that allow for the enjoyment of peace and sovereignty in our nation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: As the President of the Singapore Manufacturing Federation (SMF), I am pleased to share that SMF is an active partner of MINDEF and fully supports NS.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Through this annual event, we encourage employers to show their support for NS and the NSmen working in their organisations as well as to remind them of the important role NS plays in protecting the nation.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: Our NSmen sacrifice their time and energies to protect Singapore.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: It is important that we continue to show our appreciation to our servicemen for their commitment and contribution to defence.

speaker: Mr Douglas Foo
text: How does MINDEF continue to ensure that recognition of our NSmen remains both updated and adequate?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Mr Chairman, the SAF responded quickly to the COVID-19 situation in Singapore, mobilising our servicemen to pack masks for distribution to many households.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: As they contribute to Singapore’s fight against the virus, our servicemen’s health must be protected as well.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: Training for SAF often involves close contact, requires high physical exertion, which may lead to transmission of droplets.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: There may also be many soldiers training within a small space.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: I know that we cannot compromise our country’s security and safety by stopping the training exercises and reducing the operational readiness of our forces.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: At the same time, I am sure that we can modify some of our training procedures and processes to make sure that our men stay strong, safe and healthy.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng (Marine Parade)
text: In light of the COVID-19 outbreak, what are some of the precautionary measures that MINDEF has put in place to protect our servicemen?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Chairman, over the last few years, we have observed the trend of misinformation and falsehoods being propagated via social media networks and applications escalating.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: In some countries, the proliferation of "fake news" has even influenced the outcome of elections.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Here in Singapore, amidst the COVID-19 outbreak, we have seen several pieces of "fake news" being circulated, some of which had caused needless panic and fear among certain segments of Singaporeans.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How is MINDEF supporting whole-of-Government efforts to prepare Singaporeans to combat the spread of online falsehoods and misinformation?

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Does the Ministry have an assessment framework to determine when the spread of such online misinformation is threatening our security and at which point will the countermeasures be activated?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Chairman, over the past year, we have witnessed an increase in the number of cybersecurity breaches.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: As a response to these incidents, many countries are stepping up efforts to strengthen their cybersecurity capabilities.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin (Bukit Panjang)
text: Could I ask the Minister to provide an update on MINDEF's efforts in strengthening our cybersecurity capabilities to deter and act against potential threats?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Data security is core to Singapore’s strong defence and our continued economic success.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: As malicious threats emerge from various sources, including attempts at data exfiltration, it is essential to strengthen our capabilities and defences against these.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Digital defence is the new addition to our Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Each and every citizen has a part to play in defending our nation and our way of life, including being vigilant online.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Today, there are enemies unseen – scams, fake news and cyberattacks.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Given continual reports of security breaches worldwide, what is MINDEF doing to protect our security systems and ensure that our data and information are not compromised?

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: Many of our businesses and companies rely on secure and reliable networks to trade, transact and communicate.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: They also store vast amounts of personal and commercial data in Singapore.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: As the digital sector expands, it is important that business networks and systems are well-protected.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: We have seen the devastating impact of cyberattacks on individual businesses.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: More importantly, such attacks also could hurt Singapore's reputation as a trusted hub.

speaker: Mr Kwek Hian Chuan Henry
text: How is MINDEF working with our partners to equip businesses to deal with threats from the digital domain?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In times of increased stress on society, psychological defence is particularly salient in ensuring Singaporeans remain united in the face of external threats.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: We have seen how panic and fear can quickly disrupt our way of life.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In my main Budget speech, I spoke about the great, the wise and the good, as well as those who mock them.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: These are taken from the poem by Yeats, "Come let us mock at the Great".

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: He urged us to mock at these mockers, people who would not lift a hand to help others out of a great storm.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In light of the recent COVID-19 outbreak, it is easy to stand back, stay safe and mock others who are doing the work, taking the risks and deciding on the new rules which would keep our communities going.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: How important is our state of mind, our psychological defence?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: What can Singaporeans do to help overcome this crisis?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Mr Chairman, Sir, when Total Defence was first introduced in 1984, it was recognised that threats will not simply affect our military but potentially Singaporeans, combatants and non-combatants alike.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Thus, we must continue to build resilience in our people and community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: In order for Singapore to prevail over a threat, it is important that we fortify the resilience of the entire community.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: This concept has become more salient today, in the face of threats, such as terrorism, cyberattacks and, especially so, in face of the recent COVID-19 outbreak.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Over the years, in addition to the core pillar of Military Defence, Singapore has built up the five non-military pillars of Civil, Economic, Social, Digital and Psychological Defences to fortify the comprehensive security structure of Total Defence.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: All Singaporeans, individually and collectively, have important roles to play in our security, contributing our different expertise and abilities to build a strong and resilient nation.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: Total Defence had enabled us to overcome past challenges, such as the Severe Acute Respiratory Syndrome (SARS), terrorism and economic downturns.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: It is important that we continue to educate the next generation of Singaporeans to stay united and work together to overcome new threats.

speaker: Ms Joan Pereira
text: How is MINDEF or SAF educating our young about Total Defence?

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Mr Chairman, the success of Total Defence is contingent upon active participation and contribution by all parts of society, including the Government, businesses, communities and individuals.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: Unfortunately, the Total Defence initiatives we see today are for the most part initiated by the Government.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: We should aim to have more civic participation in Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Teo Ho Pin
text: We are in the process of encouraging more people to download this app so that they can have a crisis guide and a resource directory, all from the convenience of one's pocket.

speaker: The Chairman
text: Mr Seah Kian Peng, you can take your two cuts together.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Mr Chairman, it has been 36 years since Total Defence was launched.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Like many Singaporeans, we are all pleased to learn that MINDEF has recently launched the new Total Defence logo competition to create a new logo that represents all six pillars, including a prize money of $5,000.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: There were 10 designs that have been shortlisted and I would like to ask the Minister how did Singaporeans respond to the call for the design of the new logo?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Could the Minister also explain the significance of the new logo?

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Make no mistake, I think it is a nice design but I think it is useful and important for all to also know what goes behind the logo.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: From 1984 to last year, we have always had five pillars.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Some may say we are moving too fast in adding one more.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: I would argue that we have moved too slow.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Climate change is an existential threat to Singapore and one we need to recognise.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Not only are more of us talking about it now, we are all seeing and feeling the effects of climate change.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In my cut for the Prime Minister's Office's COS debate, I had argued that we needed a whole-of-Government approach to climate change, given its complex nature, and which straddles many Ministries.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: With changes in global trends and threats, the securitisation of technology and climate has become an existential threat to our nation.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: The Young People's Action Party (YPAP) and environmentalists have already proposed that we adopt Climate Defence as the seventh pillar of Total Defence.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: This declaration is not just a matter of policy efficiency.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: It is a matter of raising the political importance of this issue so that it will no longer be put on the backburner.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: Neither will environmental concerns be considered the poor cousin of economic growth in bureaucratic decision-making.

speaker: Mr Seah Kian Peng
text: In this Budget, we have made room for long-term planning, including for environmental issues.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Chairman, first, let me thank Members for their continued support to build a strong defence for Singapore – not only for previous Budgets, which Members have given assent, but I hope for this Budget as well – and for many of the Members for their personal commitment.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many of the Members have done their NS and, for many here, their children are doing NS, and as Mr Douglas Foo recounted, his sons.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: As he was speaking, I wished he had more sons and daughters to produce the next generation of NSmen.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The Deputy Prime Minister and Minister for Finance, in his round-up speech, reminded us of what Mr Lee Kuan Yew said our obligation was.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our greatest obligation is to the future, and sitting there, listening to Members speak, I think it is virtuous.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There were well-informed views about how difficult our external environment is – how fluid, how fast-changing, how it impacts us, how as a small country we have very little wherewithal with which to control our external events and even less to effect changes that come upon us – whether it is climate change, whether it is terrorism, whether it is factious politics in neighbouring countries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But equally, there was strong consensus and preoccupation about how to build a strong national defence.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There were good questions asked, and rightly so, about prudence, administration, about how we spend our defence dollars, how we make sure that our processes give us the maximum value and that we ensure that where we put our money, is well chosen and sustainable for our defence budget.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: What our colleagues and I will aim to do is try to answer to the best of our abilities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: First and foremost, is to give a better understanding of how MINDEF and SAF approach these questions which Members have raised.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: There is a familiar dictum in military annals – that a cardinal mistake which has led to failures has been to prepare for the next battle based on the last war.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Analysts cite this specifically for the Vietnam War, where tactics that gave the US victory in Europe during World War II proved ineffective and could not overcome the guerrilla insurgency employed by the Viet Cong.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Many Members would have seen the series on Netflix, a gripping documentary that underscores this cardinal mistake.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Singapore, as a small nation with little reserves, if caught off guard, should heed this dictum.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Vikram Nair put it rightly when he says that, "We have to be ready." But, ready for what?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We do not have the resources to plan for all eventualities.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Instead, as Members intimated, Singapore must be keenly aware of the changing circumstances around us and how they impact us.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Our region, indeed the world, is at an inflexion point, which many Members pointed out, and it is for this new environment that Singapore must prepare itself.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Internally, new military capabilities have been built and are operated by a new generation of SAF soldiers, and operated capably, I must say.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And it is because of the steadfast commitment by successive Governments and the overwhelming support from Members of this House, across party lines – Members of Parliament, Non-Constituency Members of Parliament, Nominated Members of Parliament – that we have collectively succeeded in building a strong SAF that is recognised today as a modern and professional military force, capable of defending our national interest.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Mr Douglas Foo alluded to that and Mr Charles Chong rightly put it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The very success of the SAF is that we are not tested, and indeed, that is what is said in our mission statement in the financial Budget Book – "Deterrence".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I think Miss Sylvia Lim talked about it – how the changing landscape will throw forth new threats and the SAF must be ready.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: I will go into the details of the restructuring required later.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: A new chapter has begun with elements of the old but also new principal actors.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And it is not just Asia that is fast-changing.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: When the United Kingdom (UK) government decided to allow Huawei a limited role for its 5G network, the UK dailies concluded that the US-UK relationship had become "less special".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This year's Munich Security Conference theme was meant to be provocative to prompt soul-searching, but nonetheless carried more than a modicum of insecurities – the theme was "Westlessness".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At its plenary, German President Frank-Walter Steinmeier sharply criticised the US' "America First" policy and that "Great Again" was at the expense of neighbours and partners.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The US wants the European Union (EU) to liberalise its trade policies to buy more American goods and spend more to defend themselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In response, some EU leaders do, indeed, want to reduce their dependence on the US.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Just last year, French President Emmanuel Macron put it starkly, "American decisions over the last several years... have led us to rethink fundamental diplomatic and military strategy and, on occasion, elements of solidarity which we thought were forever inalienable".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Europe is far away from Singapore, but the changes there will invariably impact our part of the world.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In the Middle East, the biggest game changer is a US that is now a net exporter of energy for the first time in nearly 70 years, and less dependent on crude oil and natural gas from the Middle East than ever before in its history.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For the first time, too, Russia has direct access to the Mediterranean Sea, and this is a warm water port in Syria, and where it can begin to build and exert military presence there.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: China, Japan and other Asian countries on the other hand, are still dependent on oil from the Middle East, through the Strait of Hormuz.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This is why President Trump remarked wryly, but not inaccurately, that the US was still "protecting the shipping lanes for other countries for zero compensation".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The US' reaction to the next Middle East crisis will be shaped by these new calculations.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The US Department of Defense (DoD), as the action arm of foreign and state policy, has made it clear that our region – the Indo Pacific – is now their "priority theatre".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Pointedly, because of China, which they characterise as a "strategic competitor" and "rival power".

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The US DoD is putting that policy in practice, and moving more ships, planes, other equipment and troops to its bases in Japan and Korea, on top of the 78,000 troops already stationed there.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Australia, a record number of US Marines deployed there last year, and the US has plans to build additional military infrastructure in Australia once Congress gives its approval.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With President Trump’s support for a bigger defence budget, such efforts will get a boost.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For China, the People’s Liberation Army’s (PLA's) expansion in blue water capability, air projection, missile and space programmes have gained momentum.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Its navy is now the world’s largest naval force, at least in numbers of ships.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Last year, China’s first indigenous aircraft carrier, the Shandong, was commissioned.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The US’ recent statements and moves are likely to accelerate, not slow down, the pace of PLA modernisation.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: European powers, too, some in heeding the US’ call and others independently, want to position themselves in Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: My counterpart, French Minister Florence Parly, has said that France, “is not going anywhere, because   part of the region”.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: True to these words, France sent its warships through the South China Sea and, in 2018, its Air Force conducted its largest-ever deployment in Southeast Asia since 2004, from Australia to India, to mark France’s presence in the region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The UK, too, has actively positioned itself in Asia.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In 2018 alone, the British Royal Navy deployed three ships to the region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Last year, the Royal Navy increased its joint military exercises with the US Navy in the South China Sea.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Asian countries, too, have beefed up their militaries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Military spending in Asia has grown more than 50% in the last decade, with both China and India in the list of top five global spenders.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: ASEAN member states have doubled their spending on defence over the last 15 years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Willy-nilly, these events, conflated, have resulted in the Asia arena becoming more militarised and contested, as Members of this House have noticed.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The South China Sea dispute adds grist to the mill, but the motivations go much deeper, that of time-old dominance in an evolving world order.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For Singapore, a small city state, 700 square kilometres, five-odd million people, we watch these developments ever so closely, carefully trying to preserve space for ourselves, to maintain our sovereignty and pursue our own interest, something which Member Desmond Choo talked about.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We have no desire to take sides or be caught in the crossfire.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And so far, we have maintained independence and space for ourselves.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But as contestation increases in this region, it will be increasingly difficult to do so.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, I appreciate Members' questions, "What will you do?

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: What will the Singapore Government do to maintain this wonderful brand of diplomacy?" Despite the challenges, Singapore was able to forge even stronger defence relations with the US, China and key partners.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And this document had underpinned defence relations between both sides for the last 30 years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: At our recent Airshow, for the first time, the Ba Yi aerobatics team performed as did the US’ F-22 and F-35B.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: With India, our militaries held bilateral exercises across all three Services under the ambit of our Bilateral Agreements and we continue to welcome India’s engagement of the region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And we were very glad that we could contribute two Chinooks and RSAF personnel to assist the Australian Defence Force during the recent bushfires.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Against the changing geopolitics, we have to watch it, we have to respond nimbly to it if we can, and we have to prepare for it.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Even so, we would need to respond to clear and present security threats, namely, three, and Members have talked about them: terrorism, cyber threats and maritime threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Against terrorism, which Ms Joan Pereira highlighted, we are not immune to the returned fighters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In fact, not only not immune, but quite vulnerable.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because there are choice targets in this region.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF will assist in this effort and work closely with other like-minded countries.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: SAF is restructuring its own military intelligence outfits, so that counter-terrorism intelligence to detect, forewarn – what Ms Joan Pereira warned about.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: We need an outfit that tells us, at least alerts us, that there are plots being undertaken.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And also responding to these plots are now part and parcel of the core mission to protect Singapore.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: It will be a key deliverable and accountability for SAF intelligence units even as they work together with other Singapore agencies dealing with this space.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Some Members asked about cybersecurity – Ms Joan Pereira, Dr Teo Ho Pin, Mr Seah Kian Peng.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: To guide the restructuring efforts required to meet security challenges, SAF and MINDEF have convened two high level committees.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: One of the committees is against cyber threats, headed by Permanent Secretary (Defence Development) and Chief of Defence Force (CDF) to spearhead this effort.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Dr Teo Ho Pin asked for updates from last year when we talked about building up a cyber force.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And basically, the challenge is to build, just like the Army, Navy and Air Force, an integrated cyber command and cyber force that can operate, defend and protect our interests in the cyber domain.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: None here, I suspect, will question the need for such a cyber force.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But in many aspects, the cyber domain is more difficult to plan and execute than in air, land and sea, and may require different types of units and force configuration.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: For air, land and sea, you have a limited number who are potential aggressors.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But in cyber, it could be potentially many more.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: So, the committee intends to be bold in examining ways that we can address this challenge but, also as important, is to recruit soldiers of the right aptitude, their training and deployments.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Because what you recruit for air, land and sea, may be different from what you need in the cyber arena.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: Nevertheless, for command integrity and accountability, after the restructuring, CDF will continue to be in charge of mission outcomes – never mind the challenges; there has to be a command structure, there has to be a Commander who is in charge, who is looking at the problem, making decisions, raising training, sustaining forces to be able to meet these challenges.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: And the Chief of Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (Chief C4I) will be the pinnacle position that holds accountability and reports directly to the CDF, similar to the other services.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF cyber command will have to provide threat assessments and early warning in cyberattacks, and also respond accordingly.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The universe of cyber threats and activists is large and the cyber command will have to prioritise its efforts and focus on key threats so as to not dissipate resources.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This restructuring effort will take some years to accomplish.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The SAF and indeed the whole of Government had made changes to better tackle maritime threats, which have expanded in recent years.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: The recent spike in sea robbery incidents in the Singapore Strait is but one example, as well as intrusions into Singapore Territorial Waters.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: These significant restructuring efforts against terrorism, cyber and maritime threats reflect the rapidly evolving spectrum of threats that today’s Singapore faces.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: But whatever the threats, for each SAF unit, effective training makes the decisive difference.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: In an uncertain landscape, we must raise, train and sustain units within the SAF to deal with both conventional and unconventional threats.

speaker: The Minister for Defence (Dr Ng Eng Hen)
text: This was a point that Mr Henry Kwek was alluding to.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For conventional operations, SAF aims to have the best training facilities globally.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we talked about conventional; we talked about unconventional.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For conventional training, our simple goal is that we want to have the best training facilities in the world.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is a high mark but we are confident we will achieve this.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some Members have asked about developments in Shoalwater Bay, Mr Charles Chong in particular.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Significant progress has been made, with completion of an ammunition storage building last year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Combined Arms Air-Land Ranges are now being developed for the Army and Air Force to train together with tanks, infantry vehicles, drones, artillery and other combined arms platforms.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This will be complemented by the Urban Operations Live Firing facilities for air and combined arms live-firing in a realistic environment.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And these facilities will be equipped with advanced targetry and instrumentation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This is a significant asset for our defence capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Charles Chong asked what will be the effect of climate change on these plans.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The short answer is probably nobody knows and we have to watch it very carefully.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There were the incidents of the bush fires this year.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And it not only will affect us but also, more impactfully, the Australian Defence Force (ADF).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Shoalwater training area, there was some halt in some activities not because there were bushfires there but because of the fear that it may accentuate it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, we are watching it very carefully, and if we have to make adjustments, we will have to.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Navy, our ships have ample opportunities to train overseas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: During Exercise Pacific Griffin, the US and our ships successfully fired the full suite of missiles, destroyed surface and air targets and hunted submarines.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We also conducted the inaugural trilateral maritime exercise in the Andaman Sea with India and Thailand.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This year, the RSN will take on a key leadership role in the world's largest multilateral maritime exercise, Rim of the Pacific Exercise (RIMPAC), alongside established navies in the Pacific Ocean.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The RSN does well in these overseas deployments that validate its systems and benchmark competencies.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Navy is also making good progress to strengthen our conventional capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The last three of the fleet of eight Littoral Mission Vessels entered into service last month.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In Germany, our new Invincible-class submarine has commenced trials in the water and her pioneer crew is undergoing work-up training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What about the Air Force, as Mr Henry Kwek asked?

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For the Air Force, the skies have opened up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In December last year, I signed an MOU with US Secretary of Defence Mark Esper to establish a fighter training detachment in Guam.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: RSAF plans to deploy our F-15s, F-16s and supporting assets, such as the Gulfstream 550 – Airborne Early Warning, to Guam for training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The airspace around Guam, together with training facilities, will allow the RSAF to conduct larger scale, more complex and realistic air-to-air and air-to-ground training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: At the same time, this detachment in Guam, alongside other deployments in Australia, India and Thailand will allow quick re-deployment back to Singapore when required.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: You can train nearer; we can bring you back if we need you.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Some have asked for an update on our acquisitions of the F-35s.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have decided on the F-35B variant of the aircraft, which can take off from a shorter runway and land vertically, and it is an important feature in land scarce Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I do not know whether it can land in one of your Housing and Development Board (HDB) car parks but we will consider this scenario.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The F-35B performed in the recent Singapore Airshow and its ability to swivel 360 degrees was simply, as some people said, "Awesome".

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We did not buy the F-35B or we did not order F-35Bs just because it can do that.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As Mr Henry Kwek rightly pointed out, it has a full suite of sensors and fighting capabilities.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have obtained the US government and Congress' assent.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Svlvia Lim raised good questions about the question marks over the F-35, and we watch it very closely.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We said we will buy four, evaluate it fully before deciding to commit on a further eight.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And our timelines are, if you like, useful to us.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I have talked about conventional and traditional operations.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We call these "grey zone" threats, as opposed to black and white.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Low-level terrorist attacks are a good example of "grey zone" threats that can turn deep black when the whole country is destabilised.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: What happened to Ukraine in the early stages is a salutary lesson on "grey zone" threats – incipient, then it cascades, extrapolates and blows up.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And when you try to mount the defence, you are finished.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, SAF has compiled the range of such "grey zone" threats.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Of course, Members will pardon me if I do not give Members a list of "grey zone" threats, and the options available to respond for each.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Each, by themselves, if limited, does not threaten our sovereignty but nevertheless can lead to instability or, cumulatively, whittle away our ability to defend national interests.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Another example of a non-traditional threat occurred, as some Members pointed out, when COVID-19 hit Singapore, that tested our Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF also helped the Ministry of Health (MOH) with contacting personnel as well as manning thermal imagery machines at the airport.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And these efforts by SAF were to enhance our psychological, social and economic resilience.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: My colleague, Senior Minister of State Mohamad Maliki will speak more on Total Defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: There is another threat for which the SAF may not be primarily responsible, but must join in the efforts for Singapore's security and safety.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And yes, I agree with Mr Seah Kian Peng that we must adopt climate defence.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Senior Minister Teo Chee Hean's Inter-Ministerial Committee on Climate Change has done very deep second, even third order work in terms of how we can step wise deal with this issue.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And I appreciate the efforts because it focuses our attention.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It also gives, to the extent available, quantitative or, if not, semi-quantitative projections of what each does.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: SAF is also making significant changes as part of the whole-of-Government (WOG) plan.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Against the effects of rising sea levels, MINDEF and SAF are working with relevant agencies closely on coastal adaptation.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Mr Chong Kee Hiong asked about the progress in Singapore's first polder development at Pulau Tekong that is led by HDB.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: As he described it, the polder comprises a dike which protects the reclaimed land from the sea and a network of drains and pumps to keep the land dry.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The tracts of land created, which are below sea level, will be used for Army training.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is early days yet, so I do not have anything concrete to report.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But obviously, this is an important project which we are learning from as we create new land for countering rising sea levels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And if this succeeds, that model and that template can be used for other areas in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF and SAF are on track to meet our national targets to reduce energy and water consumption.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It was designed to maximise natural ventilation and daylight.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I would have thought all SAF buildings were designed for natural ventilation and daylight nowadays.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But take this as what is meant, it is to maximise natural ventilation and to reduce solar heat gain.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, that is a plus now – solar heat gain and energy demand.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We have set an aim for the NS Hub to be the top 10% of energy-efficient buildings in Singapore.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The SAF is also taking discrete steps to reduce carbon emissions, even changing modes of operation without loss of any effectiveness.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: To hybrid models first, reducing emissions by up to two-thirds per vehicle, and later, when our island's infrastructure is built, with electric vehicles (EVs).

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We also established a waste management system under a joint collaboration with the National Environment Agency (NEA) and the Defence Science and Technology Agency (DSTA) that turns recycled food waste into energy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Here, a caveat, we have cut down waste.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: I noted that I have replied to a particular question on it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: It is not much waste but that is a first important thing to do.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But where there is waste, we turn it into recycled energy.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Currently, food waste collected from eight cookhouses is processed by microbes and enzymes at recycling plants to generate biogas.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And we are looking to expand this to 10 more cookhouses.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If successful, this will be expanded to all cookhouses.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: MINDEF has commissioned net-zero energy buildings at Kranji and Seletar Camps and, by the end of this financial year, the buildings in 12 of our camps will be equipped with solar panels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These measures extend to our training areas overseas as well.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: And this is in answer to Mr Charles Chong's question.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Adapting to use "green" technologies could also reap operational advantages.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: The Navy is exploring the use of hybrid propulsion systems in designing its incoming vessels.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Such technologies enable our new ships to not only reduce carbon emissions, but become more energy-efficient.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: In the grand global scheme of changes necessary to mitigate climate change, one could say that our total reduction of CO2 emissions that I just talked about might be considered insignificant, and I would agree.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But all agencies and countries must start on this road to recovery.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How will touch on some initiatives to recognise their contributions, but I mentioned earlier a second high level committee.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This committee has been formed to look at two areas – In-Camp Training (ICT) and the deployment of manpower, chaired by Deputy Secretary (Administration) and the Chief of Army.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: This committee must address the reduction in manpower and the changes necessary to fulfil the aims of the SAF, as well as to meet the needs of a new generation of NSmen, which many of you eloquently spoke for.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But we want to improve the outcome and efficiency of each ICT.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: For manpower, while we have already restructured the SAF to match the reduction in overall manpower, we do need to better match the skills and aptitude of NSmen to their vocations, as well as to make training more focused on their operational roles.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We will announce these specific changes in due course.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Last year, I informed the House about the Inspector-General’s Office (IGO) which was stood up to strengthen safety, and Senior Minister of State Heng Chee How will share and reply to some of the questions that Members have raised.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A number of Members have asked – Mr Vikram Nair, Mr Douglas Foo and Ms Sylvia Lim – whether we are able to meet our challenges with the defence spending and I would say our assessment for now is yes.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: A number of questions have been asked, how do we make sure that not only are we prudent, but that our processes give us the maximum returns for each defence dollar – Mr Douglas Foo, Ms Sylvia Lim.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: When we procure platforms or services, a thorough study is made on lifecycle costs.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Ms Sylvia Lim is quite right, I can sell you something with the low price but really dock off your dollars with high maintenance cost.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We are a little better at the game.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We put everything as lifecycle costs, so that I know the exact cost of a platform over its lifetime; a thorough study is made.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Even though we have sensitive needs for the majority of projects, it is really by open tenders to ensure competitive bidding.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: So, if you take all our contracts that the SAF and MINDEF put out, the majority are still by competitive bidding and open tenders.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: That is how we ensure we can get fair value.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But even for classified needs, we ensure that a few companies pass security requirements.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: We prequalify them, in other words, we ensure that we have more than one company that satisfies our security requirements so that they can bid competitively.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But in specific circumstances, which Ms Sylvia Lim asked about, where requirements can only be fulfilled by a single vendor, DSTA does its own stringent costing and we will compare the bid price versus our internal costing.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: If it is too far from our evaluation, whether too high or too low, we re-evaluate it.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Too high because this is not fair value.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: But too low, we are worried that you cannot deliver the product that I want.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: These processes have strengthened our procurement and, indeed, if you ask the industry and the industry is well-informed, DSTA is widely acknowledged as a "tough customer" and "reference buyer"; people have said that to me.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
text: Because when DSTA signs off on this, it tells to the whole universe of procurers that this product is value-for-money.

speaker: Dr Ng Eng Hen
